claim: Abnormal lung development can cause congenital pulmonary cysts.
source: Abnormal lung development can cause congenital pulmonary cysts, the mechanisms of which remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that establishes the context for the study.

claim: The mechanisms of congenital pulmonary cysts remain largely unknown.
source: Abnormal lung development can cause congenital pulmonary cysts, the mechanisms of which remain largely unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge about congenital pulmonary cysts.

claim: Cystic lesions are believed to result directly from disrupted airway epithelial cell growth.
source: Although the cystic lesions are believed to result directly from disrupted airway epithelial cell growth, the extent to which developmental defects in lung mesenchymal cells contribute to abnormal airway epithelial cell growth and subsequent cystic lesions has not been thoroughly examined.
evidence: This statement reflects existing beliefs in the field based on prior research.

claim: The extent to which developmental defects in lung mesenchymal cells contribute to abnormal airway epithelial cell growth and subsequent cystic lesions has not been thoroughly examined.
source: Although the cystic lesions are believed to result directly from disrupted airway epithelial cell growth, the extent to which developmental defects in lung mesenchymal cells contribute to abnormal airway epithelial cell growth and subsequent cystic lesions has not been thoroughly examined.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the current scientific literature.

claim: Abrogation of mesenchymal Bmpr1a disrupted normal lung branching morphogenesis.
source: In the present study using genetic mouse models, we dissected the roles of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor 1a (Bmpr1a)-mediated BMP signaling in lung mesenchyme during prenatal lung development and discovered that abrogation of mesenchymal Bmpr1a disrupted normal lung branching morphogenesis, leading to the formation of prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data in genetic mouse models.

claim: Abrogation of mesenchymal Bmpr1a leads to the formation of prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
source: In the present study using genetic mouse models, we dissected the roles of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor 1a (Bmpr1a)-mediated BMP signaling in lung mesenchyme during prenatal lung development and discovered that abrogation of mesenchymal Bmpr1a disrupted normal lung branching morphogenesis, leading to the formation of prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data in genetic mouse models.

claim: Severe deficiency of airway smooth muscle cells was found in the cystic airways of the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
source: Severe deficiency of airway smooth muscle cells and subepithelial elastin fibers were found in the cystic airways of the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: Severe deficiency of subepithelial elastin fibers was found in the cystic airways of the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
source: Severe deficiency of airway smooth muscle cells and subepithelial elastin fibers were found in the cystic airways of the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: Ectopic mesenchymal expression of BMP ligands was detected in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
source: In addition, ectopic mesenchymal expression of BMP ligands and airway epithelial perturbation of the Sox2-Sox9 proximal-distal axis were detected in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Airway epithelial perturbation of the Sox2-Sox9 proximal-distal axis was detected in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
source: In addition, ectopic mesenchymal expression of BMP ligands and airway epithelial perturbation of the Sox2-Sox9 proximal-distal axis were detected in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Deletion of Smad1/5 from the lung mesenchyme did not phenocopy the cystic abnormalities observed in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs.
source: However, deletion of Smad1/5, two major BMP signaling downstream effectors, from the lung mesenchyme did not phenocopy the cystic abnormalities observed in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs, suggesting that a Smad-independent mechanism contributes to prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data comparing different knockout models.

claim: A Smad-independent mechanism contributes to prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
source: However, deletion of Smad1/5, two major BMP signaling downstream effectors, from the lung mesenchyme did not phenocopy the cystic abnormalities observed in the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout lungs, suggesting that a Smad-independent mechanism contributes to prenatal pulmonary cystic lesions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that Smad1/5 deletion did not reproduce the phenotype.

claim: Mesenchymal BMP signaling plays a role in lung development.
source: These findings reveal for the first time the role of mesenchymal BMP signaling in lung development and a potential pathogenic mechanism underlying congenital pulmonary cysts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Congenital pulmonary cysts cause respiratory distress, infection, and pneumothorax in neonates.
source: Congenital pulmonary cysts, resulting from abnormal fetal lung development, cause respiratory distress, infection, and pneumothorax in neonates.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge about congenital pulmonary cysts.

claim: The dynamic pathogenic process and mechanisms of congenital pulmonary cysts are difficult to study in humans.
source: The dynamic pathogenic process and mechanisms are difficult to study in humans and few animal models are available.
evidence: This reflects the practical challenges in studying this condition.

claim: Few animal models are available for studying congenital pulmonary cysts.
source: The dynamic pathogenic process and mechanisms are difficult to study in humans and few animal models are available.
evidence: This reflects the current state of research tools available.

claim: Lung development begins with the specification of the respiratory domain in the ventral wall of the anterior foregut endoderm, as indicated by the expression of Nkx2-1.
source: It is known that lung development begins with the specification of the respiratory domain in the ventral wall of the anterior foregut endoderm, as indicated by the expression of Nkx2-1, and the separation of the respiratory tract from the dorsal esophagus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lung development.

claim: The primary lung epithelial buds undergo reiterated elongation and division to form the conducting airways (branching morphogenesis).
source: The primary lung epithelial buds then undergo reiterated elongation and division to form the conducting airways (branching morphogenesis), followed by distal saccular formation and peripheral alveolarization to give rise to millions of gas exchange units (McCulley et al., 2015; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lung development supported by citations.

claim: Lung morphogenesis is a complex process relying on the highly coordinated development of both lung epithelium and lung mesenchyme.
source: It is notable that lung morphogenesis is a complex process relying on the highly coordinated development of both lung epithelium and lung mesenchyme.
evidence: This is a statement reflecting current understanding of lung development.

claim: Lung mesenchymal lineages, including airway and vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs), pericytes, and stromal fibroblasts, are as important as epithelial cells in proper lung development.
source: Evidence has increasingly suggested that lung mesenchymal lineages, including airway and vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs), pericytes, and stromal fibroblasts, are as important as epithelial cells in proper lung development (Noe et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The lung mesenchyme provides a microenvironment that regulates the growth of epithelium through a variety of morphogenic signals, such as Wnts, fibroblast growth factors (Fgfs), and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs).
source: In addition to acting as a mechanical framework that supports the formation of the bronchi, bronchioles, and the distal alveoli, the lung mesenchyme provides a microenvironment that regulates the growth of epithelium through a variety of morphogenic signals, such as Wnts, fibroblast growth factors (Fgfs), and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) (McCulley et al., 2015; Nikolić et al., 2018; Morrisey et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BMPs are a family of growth factors that direct many biological processes, including organogenesis.
source: BMPs are a family of growth factors that direct many biological processes, including organogenesis (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: BMPs bind to the receptor complex of BMP receptor II (Bmpr2) and BMP receptor I (Bmpr1a or Bmpr1b), which in turn activates the intracellular Smad-dependent and Smad-independent pathways.
source: BMPs bind to the receptor complex of BMP receptor II (Bmpr2) and BMP receptor I (Bmpr1a or Bmpr1b), which in turn activates the intracellular Smad-dependent and Smad-independent pathways (Shi and Massagué, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BMP signaling supported by a citation.

claim: Mice with conventional Bmpr1a gene deletions are early embryonic lethal (E7.5–9.5) before lung organogenesis.
source: Mice with conventional Bmpr1a gene deletions are early embryonic lethal (E7.5–9.5) before lung organogenesis (Mishina et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a finding from previous research supported by a citation.

claim: Both hyperactivation and inhibition of BMP signaling in fetal lung epithelial cells result in lung malformation, which is primarily due to the defects in distal lung epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation/maturation.
source: As reported by us and other groups, both hyperactivation and inhibition of BMP signaling in fetal lung epithelial cells result in lung malformation, which is primarily due to the defects in distal lung epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation/maturation (Luo et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2008; Weaver et al., 1999; Bellusci et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research including the authors' own work.

claim: The role of mesenchymal BMP signaling in regulating fetal lung development has not been studied due to the lack of lung mesenchyme-specific targeting tools in the past.
source: However, the role of mesenchymal BMP signaling in regulating fetal lung development has not been studied due to the lack of lung mesenchyme-specific targeting tools in the past.
evidence: This identifies a gap in previous research due to technical limitations.

claim: A lung mesenchyme-specific Tbx4 lung enhancer-driven loxP/Cre mouse driver line was recently generated.
source: We recently generated a lung mesenchyme-specific Tbx4 lung enhancer-driven loxP/Cre mouse driver line (Zhang et al., 2013) which enables us to manipulate BMP signaling specifically in lung mesenchymal cells in vivo and to study its role in the lung development.
evidence: This is a methodological development reported by the authors with a citation.

claim: Bmpr1a is expressed predominantly in fetal mouse lung airway epithelial cells at the early gestation stage (embryonic day [E]12.5 to E14.5).
source: Although Bmpr1a is expressed predominantly in fetal mouse lung airway epithelial cells at the early gestation stage (embryonic day [E]12.5 to E14.5), its expression in fetal lung mesenchyme is also evident during mid-gestation (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from previous research supported by a citation.

claim: Bmpr1a expression in fetal lung mesenchyme is evident during mid-gestation.
source: Although Bmpr1a is expressed predominantly in fetal mouse lung airway epithelial cells at the early gestation stage (embryonic day [E]12.5 to E14.5), its expression in fetal lung mesenchyme is also evident during mid-gestation (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from previous research supported by a citation.

claim: Specific deletion of Bmpr1a in fetal lung mesenchymal cells resulted in abnormal airway development and subsequent prenatal cystic malformation.
source: Herein, we specifically deleted Bmpr1a in fetal lung mesenchymal cells, which resulted in abnormal airway development and subsequent prenatal cystic malformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The pathological phenotype of mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout resembles the features observed in pediatric patients diagnosed with congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM).
source: This pathological phenotype resembles the features observed in pediatric patients diagnosed with congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM).
evidence: This is a comparison between the mouse model phenotype and human disease.

claim: Bmpr1a was specifically knocked out in the lung mesenchyme with doxycycline (Dox) induction from the beginning of lung formation (E6.5).
source: By crossing the Tbx4-rtTA/TetO-Cre driver line to the floxed-Bmpr1a mice (Tbx4-rtTA/TetO-Cre/Bmpr1afx/fx), Bmpr1a was specifically knocked out in the lung mesenchyme with doxycycline (Dox) induction from the beginning of lung formation (E6.5, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study, validated by data shown in the figure.

claim: Bmpr1a knockout in lung mesenchyme was validated at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: This was validated at the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In E15.5 mesenchyme-specific Bmpr1a conditional knockout (CKO), Bmpr1a immunostaining was absent in lung mesenchyme but present in the epithelia.
source: For example, in E15.5 mesenchyme-specific Bmpr1a conditional knockout (CKO), Bmpr1a immunostaining was absent in lung mesenchyme but present in the epithelia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) while Bmpr1a was detected in both mesenchyme and epithelia of wildtype (WT) lungs.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Early embryonic lung morphogenesis between Bmpr1a CKO lungs and WT controls was comparable prior to E13.5.
source: By gross view with quantitative analysis (Figure 1A–C), early embryonic lung morphogenesis between Bmpr1a CKO lungs and WT controls was comparable prior to E13.5.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and images shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Decreased epithelial branching and increased size of branching tips were observed from E14.5 in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: Decreased epithelial branching and increased size of branching tips were observed from E14.5.
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: As lung development progressed, the terminal airways in Bmpr1a CKO lungs displayed dilation and exhibited increasingly extensive cystic changes.
source: As lung development progressed, the terminal airways in Bmpr1a CKO lungs displayed dilation and exhibited increasingly extensive cystic changes.
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The overall size of the lungs remained relatively unchanged in Bmpr1a CKO mice.
source: However, the overall size of the lungs remained relatively unchanged.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The walls of the lung cysts were lined with a single layer of epithelial cells.
source: The walls of the lung cysts were lined with a single layer of epithelial cells, over the course of development, ultimately resulting in the formation of balloon-like cystic lesions by the end of gestation (E18.5).
evidence: This is a histological observation from the study shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Balloon-like cystic lesions formed by the end of gestation (E18.5) in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: The walls of the lung cysts were lined with a single layer of epithelial cells, over the course of development, ultimately resulting in the formation of balloon-like cystic lesions by the end of gestation (E18.5).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overall cell proliferation at E15.5 had no significant change between cystic Bmpr1a CKO and WT control lungs as measured by EdU labeling.
source: Interestingly, overall cell proliferation and apoptosis at E15.5, when lung cysts were developed, had no significant change between cystic Bmpr1a CKO and WT control lungs as measured by EdU labeling and TUNEL assay, respectively (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Overall apoptosis at E15.5 had no significant change between cystic Bmpr1a CKO and WT control lungs as measured by TUNEL assay.
source: Interestingly, overall cell proliferation and apoptosis at E15.5, when lung cysts were developed, had no significant change between cystic Bmpr1a CKO and WT control lungs as measured by EdU labeling and TUNEL assay, respectively (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A total of 1001 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between Bmpr1a CKO and WT lung tissues at E15.5.
source: A total of 1001 DEGs (false discovery rate [FDR] ≤ 0.05 and log2FC [fold change]  ≥ 1) were identified, among which 547 genes were upregulated and 454 genes were downregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs as compared to the transcriptome of WT lungs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: 547 genes were upregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs compared to WT lungs.
source: A total of 1001 DEGs (false discovery rate [FDR] ≤ 0.05 and log2FC [fold change]  ≥ 1) were identified, among which 547 genes were upregulated and 454 genes were downregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs as compared to the transcriptome of WT lungs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: 454 genes were downregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs compared to WT lungs.
source: A total of 1001 DEGs (false discovery rate [FDR] ≤ 0.05 and log2FC [fold change]  ≥ 1) were identified, among which 547 genes were upregulated and 454 genes were downregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs as compared to the transcriptome of WT lungs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Lung mesenchymal Bmpr1a regulates a large number of genes involved in the Muscle System Process (p<0.001).
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that lung mesenchymal Bmpr1a regulates a large number of genes involved in the Muscle System Process (p<0.001, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Enlarged airways were initially seen in Bmpr1a CKO lungs from E14.5.
source: As shown above in Figure 1, enlarged airways were initially seen in Bmpr1a CKO lungs from E14.5.
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A specific absence of airway SMCs was found surrounding the dilated airway branching in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: Whole mount staining of smooth muscle actin and comprehensive 3D imaging revealed a specific absence of airway SMCs surrounding the dilated airway branching in Bmpr1a CKO lungs, while unaffected airway branches in Bmpr1a CKO lungs remained surrounded by SMCs, as compared to the WT lungs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by whole mount staining and 3D imaging data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Unaffected airway branches in Bmpr1a CKO lungs remained surrounded by SMCs.
source: Whole mount staining of smooth muscle actin and comprehensive 3D imaging revealed a specific absence of airway SMCs surrounding the dilated airway branching in Bmpr1a CKO lungs, while unaffected airway branches in Bmpr1a CKO lungs remained surrounded by SMCs, as compared to the WT lungs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by whole mount staining and 3D imaging data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Reduction and even lack of airway SMCs was consistently found around the enlarged airways of E15.5 Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: As lung development proceeded to E15.5, the distal airway enlargement became increasingly severe and extensive, as indicated by the whole mount staining of Cdh1 (E-cadherin), which outlines the airway epithelia. Reduction and even lack of airway SMCs was consistently found around the enlarged airways of E15.5 Bmpr1a CKO lungs, shown by immunostaining for SMC markers Acta2 and Myh11 (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Vascular SMCs in Bmpr1a CKO lungs appeared to remain unaffected.
source: In contrast, vascular SMCs in Bmpr1a CKO lungs appeared to remain unaffected (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Bmpr1a deletion in pericytes and endothelial cells had no effects on these cells or the associated pulmonary vasculature.
source: However, Bmpr1a deletion in these cell lineages had no effects on these cells or the associated pulmonary vasculature, as measured by the relevant cellular markers (Cspg4 and Pecam1) at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Several major components of the ECM in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs, such as laminin and type III collagen, had no significant changes at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Several major components of the ECM in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs, such as laminin and type III collagen, were examined at both the mRNA and protein levels. No significant changes were found, even in the areas surrounding the dilated airways and lung cysts when compared to the WT lungs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The mesenchymal knockout of Bmpr1a caused significant reduction of elastin expression, as detected by real-time PCR and western blot.
source: However, the mesenchymal knockout of Bmpr1a caused significant reduction of elastin expression, as detected by real-time PCR and western blot (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The decrease in elastin expression in Bmpr1a CKO lungs occurred primarily in the areas adjacent to the epithelia of enlarged airways with the deficiency of airway smooth muscle.
source: In the Bmpr1a CKO lungs, co-immunostaining of epithelia (Cdh1), SMCs (Acta2), and elastin (Eln) showed that this decrease in elastin expression occurred primarily in the areas adjacent to the epithelia of enlarged airways with the deficiency of airway smooth muscle.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant increase in elastin protein was observed in fetal lung mesenchymal cells treated with BMP4.
source: To determine whether BMP signaling can directly regulate elastin expression in fetal lung mesenchymal cells, alteration of elastin protein expression upon BMP4 treatment in primary fetal lung mesenchymal cells was analyzed. A significant increase in elastin protein was observed in the cells treated with BMP4 (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Inclusion of the BMP type 1 receptor (BMPR1) inhibitor LDN193189 (LDN) fully blocked the BMP4-stimulated elastin upregulation.
source: However, inclusion of the BMP type 1 receptor (BMPR1) inhibitor LDN193189 (LDN) fully blocked the BMP4-stimulated elastin upregulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The downregulation of Smad1/5-mediated BMP signaling was observed in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs, evident from the reduced phosphorylation of Smad1/5.
source: In line with this report, the downregulation of Smad1/5-mediated BMP signaling was also observed in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs, evident from the reduced phosphorylation of Smad1/5 (p-Samd1/5 in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Treatment of fetal lung mesenchymal cells with BMP4 activated Smad1/5 phosphorylation.
source: Treatment of these cells with BMP4 activated Smad1/5 phosphorylation, while the addition of BMPR1 inhibitor LDN reduced the BMP4-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Addition of BMPR1 inhibitor LDN reduced the BMP4-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation in fetal lung mesenchymal cells.
source: Treatment of these cells with BMP4 activated Smad1/5 phosphorylation, while the addition of BMPR1 inhibitor LDN reduced the BMP4-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Abnormal fetal lungs with hypoplastic development were present in the Smad1/5 double CKO mice.
source: Although abnormal fetal lungs with hypoplastic development were present in the Smad1/5 double CKO mice, airway dilation and cystic lesions were not detected (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Airway dilation and cystic lesions were not detected in Smad1/5 double CKO mice.
source: Although abnormal fetal lungs with hypoplastic development were present in the Smad1/5 double CKO mice, airway dilation and cystic lesions were not detected (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In the Smad1/5 CKO lungs, airway SMC growth was not affected, as indicated by the expression of Acta2 around the airways.
source: Furthermore, in the Smad1/5 CKO lungs, airway SMC growth was not affected, as indicated by the expression of Acta2 around the airways (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Airway SMC growth may be independent of Smad1/5-mediated pathway.
source: This different phenotypic observation suggests that airway SMC growth may be independent of Smad1/5-mediated pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Smad1/5 deletion did not affect airway SMC growth.

claim: Reduced phosphorylation of p38 (p-p38) mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), but not Jnk and Erk, was detected in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: We then examined other major Smad-independent pathways in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs. Reduced phosphorylation of p38 (p-p38) mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), but not Jnk and Erk, was detected in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Bmp4 treatment of cultured primary lung mesenchymal progenitor cells specifically activated p38.
source: Bmp4 treatment of the cultured primary lung mesenchymal progenitor cells also specifically activated p38, a response that was specifically blocked by the addition of the BMPR1 inhibitor LDN (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Addition of the BMPR1 inhibitor LDN blocked the BMP4-induced p38 activation in cultured primary lung mesenchymal progenitor cells.
source: Bmp4 treatment of the cultured primary lung mesenchymal progenitor cells also specifically activated p38, a response that was specifically blocked by the addition of the BMPR1 inhibitor LDN (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Myocd is a key transcription co-factor in controlling airway SMC differentiation.
source: As previously reported (Young et al., 2020), Myocd is a key transcription co-factor in controlling airway SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Treatment of lung mesenchymal progenitor cells with BMP4 induced a pronounced increase in the expression of SMC-related genes at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Treatment of lung mesenchymal progenitor cells with BMP4 induced a pronounced increase in the expression of these SMC-related genes at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Inhibition of either Bmpr1a by LDN or p38 by SB203580 (SB) significantly attenuated the promoting effect of BMP4 on SMC differentiation.
source: Inhibition of either Bmpr1a by LDN or p38 by SB203580 (SB) significantly attenuated the promoting effect of BMP4 on SMC differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: BMP4 treatment could promote SMC-associated gene expression in lung SMCs of non-vascular origin rather than those of vascular origin, as assessed by their Myh11 expression.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, BMP4 treatment could promote SMC-associated gene expression in lung SMCs of non-vascular origin rather than those of vascular origin, as assessed by their Myh11 expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The BMP4-induced upregulation of Myh11 expression in non-vascular SMCs was effectively blocked by concurrent treatment with the BMP type 1 receptor-specific inhibitor LDN.
source: This BMP4-induced upregulation of Myh11 expression in non-vascular SMCs was effectively blocked by concurrent treatment with the BMP type 1 receptor-specific inhibitor LDN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Previous studies using embryonic lung explant culture have suggested that airway SMCs play an important role in branching morphogenesis in developmental lungs.
source: Previous studies using embryonic lung explant culture have suggested that airway SMCs play an important role in branching morphogenesis in developmental lungs (Kim et al., 2015; Jesudason, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myocd encodes an important transcriptional coactivator of serum response factor, modulating the expression of smooth muscle-specific cytoskeletal and contractile proteins.
source: Myocd encodes an important transcriptional coactivator of serum response factor, modulating the expression of smooth muscle-specific cytoskeletal and contractile proteins (Parmacek, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Expression of Myocd was substantially downregulated in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: In our Bmpr1a CKO lungs, expression of Myocd was substantially downregulated (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Knockout of Myocd led to a severe deficiency in airway SMC development.
source: As detected by Acta2 immunostaining, knockout of Myocd led to a severe deficiency in airway SMC development (Figure 6B) resembling the airway SMC deficiency observed in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs (Figures 2 and 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Mesenchymal Bmpr1a expression remained unchanged in the Myocd CKO lungs.
source: However, mesenchymal Bmpr1a expression remained unchanged in the Myocd CKO lungs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: No significant branching defect or cystic malformation was observed in the Myocd CKO lungs.
source: However, mesenchymal Bmpr1a expression remained unchanged in the Myocd CKO lungs (Figure 6C). No significant branching defect or cystic malformation was observed in the Myocd CKO lungs (Figure 6D), which is consistent with the previous report (Young et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure and consistent with a cited previous report.

claim: Despite severe disruption of airway SMC development in the Myocd CKO lungs, elastin fiber deposition in the airways was unaffected.
source: Despite severe disruption of airway SMC development in the Myocd CKO lungs, elastin fiber deposition in the airways was unaffected (Figure 6B), which was a significant difference when compared to the findings in the Bmpr1a CKO airways, where a deficiency of elastin fibers adjacent to the epithelium was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Sox2-positive epithelial cells were barely detected in the proximal airways of Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: Interestingly, in the Bmpr1a CKO lung, Sox2-positive epithelial cells were barely detected in the proximal airways.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Lack of further differentiation of Foxj1-positive cells was observed in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: Similarly, lack of further differentiation of Foxj1-positive cells was also observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells expressing Sox9 and Sftpc, which are normally confined to the distal epithelial cells during lung branching, were expanded to the proximal region of the airways in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: In contrast, cells expressing Sox9 and Sftpc, which are normally confined to the distal epithelial cells during lung branching, were expanded to the proximal region of the airways in Bmpr1a CKO lungs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout downregulated multiple proximal airway epithelial marker genes.
source: The analysis of tissue RNA-seq data revealed that the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout downregulated multiple proximal airway epithelial marker genes, while various distal airway epithelial marker genes were upregulated (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout upregulated various distal airway epithelial marker genes.
source: The analysis of tissue RNA-seq data revealed that the mesenchymal Bmpr1a knockout downregulated multiple proximal airway epithelial marker genes, while various distal airway epithelial marker genes were upregulated (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Ectopic expression of Bmp4 in fetal mouse lung has been reported to cause distal epithelial expansion.
source: Ectopic expression of Bmp4 in fetal mouse lung has been reported to cause distal epithelial expansion (Bellusci et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased expression of Bmp4 in E15.5 Bmpr1a CKO lungs was initially found by RNA-seq and validated by RT-PCR.
source: Increased expression of Bmp4 in E15.5 Bmpr1a CKO lungs was initially found by RNA-seq (logFC>1, GEO#: GSE97946) and validated by RT-PCR (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The inverse relationship between Bmpr1a deletion (intracellular BMP signaling) and Bmp4 ligand expression in fetal lung mesenchymal progenitor cells was confirmed by comparing Bmp4 expression in isolated fetal lung mesenchymal cells with different Bmpr1a genotypes.
source: The inverse relationship between Bmpr1a deletion (intracellular BMP signaling) and Bmp4 ligand expression in these fetal lung mesenchymal progenitor cells was further confirmed by comparing Bmp4 expression in isolated fetal lung mesenchymal cells with different Bmpr1a genotypes (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Alterations of other key pathways including Fgf, Wnt, and Shh were not detected by RNA-seq and RT-PCR through analyzing the related targeted genes.
source: Alterations of other key pathways including Fgf, Wnt, and Shh were not detected by RNA-seq and RT-PCR through analyzing the related targeted genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Bmpr1a-mediated BMP signaling in lung mesenchymal cells is indispensable in lung development.
source: Our current study provides solid in vivo evidence for the first time that Bmpr1a-mediated BMP signaling in lung mesenchymal cells is indispensable in lung development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Lung mesenchymal deletion of Bmpr1a at an early developmental stage causes abnormal branching morphogenesis and then severe lung cysts at late gestation in mice.
source: Lung mesenchymal deletion of Bmpr1a at an early developmental stage causes abnormal branching morphogenesis and then severe lung cysts at late gestation in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: Congenital pulmonary cysts are reported in human CPAM patients as a result of abnormal prenatal lung development.
source: Interestingly, congenital pulmonary cysts are reported in human CPAM patients as a result of abnormal prenatal lung development (Stocker, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reduction of airway SMCs and decreased subepithelial elastin fibers are the common pathological changes in the cystic airways of human CPAM samples.
source: Reduction of airway SMCs and decreased subepithelial elastin fibers are also found to be the common pathological changes in the cystic airways of human CPAM samples (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Studies in mouse models suggest that altered growth factor signaling in a prenatal time window is sufficient to cause cyst formation.
source: Studies in mouse models suggest that altered growth factor signaling in a prenatal time window is sufficient to cause cyst formation (Miao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Integrated suppression of BMP signaling pathway was recently found in human CPAM specimens by an RNA-seq approach.
source: Interestingly, integrated suppression of BMP signaling pathway was recently found in human CPAM specimens by an RNA-seq approach (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Epithelial overexpression of Bmp4 appears to induce extensive mesenchymal SMC differentiation in vivo.
source: It has been reported that epithelial overexpression of Bmp4 appears to induce extensive mesenchymal SMC differentiation in vivo (Badri et al., 2008), and that BMP4 promotes myocyte differentiation and inhibits cell proliferation in cultured human fetal lung fibroblasts via the Smad1 pathway (Jeffery et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BMP4 promotes myocyte differentiation and inhibits cell proliferation in cultured human fetal lung fibroblasts via the Smad1 pathway.
source: It has been reported that epithelial overexpression of Bmp4 appears to induce extensive mesenchymal SMC differentiation in vivo (Badri et al., 2008), and that BMP4 promotes myocyte differentiation and inhibits cell proliferation in cultured human fetal lung fibroblasts via the Smad1 pathway (Jeffery et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Smad1 and Smad5 are critical downstream effectors of BMP type I receptors, mediating BMP canonical signal pathway.
source: Smad1 and Smad5 are critical downstream effectors of BMP type I receptors, mediating BMP canonical signal pathway (Wang et al., 2014; Katagiri and Watabe, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Simultaneous deletion of Smad1 and Smad5 in mouse lung mesenchyme does not affect the differentiation of airway SMCs although it disrupts early embryonic lung morphogenesis.
source: However, our in vivo study indicates that simultaneous deletion of Smad1 and Smad5 in mouse lung mesenchyme does not affect the differentiation of airway SMCs although it disrupts early embryonic lung morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The decrease in phosphorylated Smad1 and Smad5 in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs is not responsible for the defective airway SMC growth.
source: This suggests that the decrease in phosphorylated Smad1 and Smad5 in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs is not responsible for the defective airway SMC growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Smad1/5 deletion did not affect airway SMC growth.

claim: BMP-activated Bmp receptors also function through MAPK.
source: In addition to the Smad-dependent BMP signal pathway, BMP-activated Bmp receptors also function through MAPK (Wang et al., 2014; Katagiri and Watabe, 2016; von Bubnoff and Cho, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: p38 MAPK regulates cell proliferation in a variety of SMC types, including airway SMCs.
source: Many studies have shown that p38 MAPK regulates cell proliferation in a variety of SMC types, including airway SMCs (Chen and Khalil, 2006; Pelaia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The p38 MAPK is involved in myogenic differentiation and myofibroblast trans-differentiation.
source: The p38 MAPK is also involved in myogenic differentiation and myofibroblast trans-differentiation (Choi et al., 2011; Meyer-Ter-Vehn et al., 2006; Sebe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: p38 is the primary intracellular signaling component to mediate BMP's regulatory effects on airway myogenesis.
source: This suggests that p38 is the primary intracellular signaling component to mediate BMP's regulatory effects on airway myogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing p38 activation by BMP4 and its role in SMC differentiation.

claim: Airway and vascular SMCs seem to originate from distinct mesenchymal progenitor populations.
source: Despite being commonly characterized by the expression of a variety of myogenesis-associated genes, airway and vascular SMCs seem to originate from distinct mesenchymal progenitor populations (Zhang et al., 2013), and are regulated by distinct molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Myocd is abundant in airway SMCs but barely expressed in vascular SMCs.
source: Our previous study has demonstrated that Myocd is abundant in airway SMCs but barely expressed in vascular SMCs (Young et al., 2020), and that cardiovascular SMC development is mediated by myocardin-related transcription factors, the other members of Myocd family (Parmacek, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research including the authors' own work.

claim: Cardiovascular SMC development is mediated by myocardin-related transcription factors, the other members of Myocd family.
source: Our previous study has demonstrated that Myocd is abundant in airway SMCs but barely expressed in vascular SMCs (Young et al., 2020), and that cardiovascular SMC development is mediated by myocardin-related transcription factors, the other members of Myocd family (Parmacek, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hypomorphic FGF-10 mice only display decreased expression of airway smooth muscle actin.
source: For instance, hypomorphic FGF-10 mice only display decreased expression of airway smooth muscle actin (Mailleux et al., 2005), while deletion of Wnt-7b selectively disrupts the development of vascular SMCs (Shu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Deletion of Wnt-7b selectively disrupts the development of vascular SMCs.
source: For instance, hypomorphic FGF-10 mice only display decreased expression of airway smooth muscle actin (Mailleux et al., 2005), while deletion of Wnt-7b selectively disrupts the development of vascular SMCs (Shu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reduced expression of Bmpr1a is associated with various forms of acquired as well as primary nonfamilial pulmonary hypertension.
source: Although reduced expression of Bmpr1a is associated with various forms of acquired as well as primary nonfamilial pulmonary hypertension (Du et al., 2003), the role of Bmpr1a-mediated signaling in regulating prenatal lung vascular SMC development has not been studied.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bmpr1a is dispensable in fetal vascular SMC development.
source: Our current data suggest that Bmpr1a is dispensable in fetal vascular SMC development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Airway SMCs initially develop from local mesenchymal cells around the tips of epithelial buds undergoing bifurcation.
source: Previous studies have suggested that airway SMCs initially develop from local mesenchymal cells around the tips of epithelial buds undergoing bifurcation. These cells wrap around the bifurcating cleft and neck of the terminal buds, and then grow rigidly alongside the elongating bronchial tree (Kim et al., 2015; Badri et al., 2008; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inhibition of SMC differentiation in embryonic lung explant culture prevented airway terminal bifurcation.
source: Inhibition of SMC differentiation in embryonic lung explant culture, such as by blocking L-type Ca2+ channels using nifedipine, or by inhibiting FGF and SHH signaling using SU5402SHH and cyclopamine, prevented airway terminal bifurcation (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Abrogation of airway SMCs by deleting mesenchymal Myocd does not cause any significant abnormalities in airway branching morphogenesis.
source: However, our current and a recently published study demonstrate that abrogation of airway SMCs by deleting mesenchymal Myocd does not cause any significant abnormalities in airway branching morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study and a cited recent study.

claim: Loss of SMCs is neither the primary nor sole mechanism accounting for the reduction of airway branching, dilation of terminal airways, and development of airway cysts in Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
source: This suggests that loss of SMCs is neither the primary nor sole mechanism accounting for the reduction of airway branching, dilation of terminal airways, and development of airway cysts in our Bmpr1a CKO lungs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Myocd deletion caused SMC loss but not cystic lesions.

claim: Elastin expression in the developing lung parenchyma prior to alveologenesis is predominantly localized to the mesenchyme in the developing airways.
source: Interestingly, elastin expression in the developing lung parenchyma prior to alveologenesis is predominantly localized to the mesenchyme in the developing airways, as indicated by our elastin immunostaining data, suggesting that elastin plays a role in airway branching.
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by immunostaining data.

claim: The perinatal development of terminal airway branches is arrested in mice lacking elastin (Eln -/-), resulting in dilated distal air sacs that form abnormally large cavities.
source: Previous study has revealed that the perinatal development of terminal airway branches is arrested in mice lacking elastin (Eln -/-), resulting in dilated distal air sacs that form abnormally large cavities (Wendel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Airway smooth muscles are normal in elastin null mice.
source: It is worthy to note that airway smooth muscles are normal in these elastin null mice, implying that loss of elastic fiber alone is not sufficient to cause airway cystic pathology, but could serve as an additional factor contributing to the lesions in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from previous research that is used to support an inference.

claim: Loss of elastic fiber alone is not sufficient to cause airway cystic pathology, but could serve as an additional factor contributing to the lesions in vivo.
source: It is worthy to note that airway smooth muscles are normal in these elastin null mice, implying that loss of elastic fiber alone is not sufficient to cause airway cystic pathology, but could serve as an additional factor contributing to the lesions in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that elastin null mice have normal airway smooth muscles.

claim: Congenital airway cysts in the lungs of human CPAM patients are characterized by compromised smooth muscle and elastin fiber.
source: This assumption is also supported by the fact that congenital airway cysts in the lungs of human CPAM patients are characterized by compromised smooth muscle and elastin fiber (Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Disruption of BMP signaling by LDN-193189 can substantially improve Bmp4 production.
source: Previous studies have shown that disruption of BMP signaling by LDN-193189 can substantially improve Bmp4 production (Kim and Lee, 2019), and that deletion of Bmpr1a and Acvr1 in the lens-forming ectoderm increases Bmp2, -4, and -7 transcripts (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Deletion of Bmpr1a and Acvr1 in the lens-forming ectoderm increases Bmp2, -4, and -7 transcripts.
source: Previous studies have shown that disruption of BMP signaling by LDN-193189 can substantially improve Bmp4 production (Kim and Lee, 2019), and that deletion of Bmpr1a and Acvr1 in the lens-forming ectoderm increases Bmp2, -4, and -7 transcripts (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Misexpression of BMP4 results in a decrease of Sox2+ proximal progenitors and an expansion of Sox9+/Id2+ distal progenitors in fetal mouse lungs, leading to malformed airways.
source: Misexpression of BMP4 results in a decrease of Sox2+ proximal progenitors and an expansion of Sox9+/Id2+ distal progenitors in fetal mouse lungs, leading to malformed airways (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Overexpression of Bmp antagonist Xnoggin or gremlin in fetal distal lung epithelium leads to a severe reduction of distal epithelial cell types and a concurrent expanded expression of the proximal epithelial cell markers CC10 and Foxj1.
source: Consistently, overexpression of Bmp antagonist Xnoggin or gremlin in fetal distal lung epithelium leads to a severe reduction of distal epithelial cell types and a concurrent expanded expression of the proximal epithelial cell markers CC10 and Foxj1 (Weaver et al., 1999; Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The lung mesenchyme is closely involved in respiratory lineage specification and epithelial differentiation by producing many critical signaling molecules, such as Bmp ligands, that direct endodermal expression of specific cell markers in a temporal and spatial fashion.
source: Evidence increasingly suggests that the lung mesenchyme is closely involved in respiratory lineage specification and epithelial differentiation by producing many critical signaling molecules, such as Bmp ligands, that direct endodermal expression of specific cell markers in a temporal and spatial fashion (McCulley et al., 2015; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The decrease in proximal cell types and ectopic expression of distal cell markers (Sox9) in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs may be subsequently caused by abnormal increase of Bmp ligands.
source: Therefore, the decrease in proximal cell types and ectopic expression of distal cell markers (Sox9) in the Bmpr1a CKO lungs may be subsequently caused by abnormal increase of Bmp ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed increase in Bmp ligands and the known effects of BMP signaling on epithelial patterning.

claim: Loss of Sox2+ or expansion of Sox9+ in airway epithelia are associated with altered epithelial differentiation and branching, as well as cystic pathology in fetal lungs.
source: This aberrant epithelial growth may also contribute to airway cyst formation, as multiple mouse models have suggested that loss of Sox2+ or expansion of Sox9+ in airway epithelia are associated with altered epithelial differentiation and branching, as well as cystic pathology in fetal lungs (Wang et al., 2013; Liberti et al., 2019; Rockich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mesenchymal Bmpr1a is essential for lung development, particularly airway branching morphogenesis.
source: In summary, mesenchymal Bmpr1a is essential for lung development, particularly airway branching morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Disruption of Bmpr1a-mediated mesenchymal signaling causes prenatal airway malformation and cystic lesions.
source: Disruption of Bmpr1a-mediated mesenchymal signaling causes prenatal airway malformation and cystic lesions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Multiple mechanisms, including deficiency of airway smooth muscle, airway elastin fiber defect, and perturbation of the Sox2-Sox9 epithelial progenitor axis, may contribute to the congenital airway cystic pathogenesis.
source: Multiple mechanisms, including deficiency of airway smooth muscle, airway elastin fiber defect, and perturbation of the Sox2-Sox9 epithelial progenitor axis, may contribute to the congenital airway cystic pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: The downstream Smad-independent p38 pathway appears to be critical in mediating BMP-regulated airway smooth muscle development.
source: In addition, the downstream Smad-independent p38 pathway appears to be critical in mediating BMP-regulated airway smooth muscle development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.
